papers.title: Enteric alpha-synuclein pathology in early-onset parkinsonism: Findings in a patient with SCA6.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: In Parkinson's disease (PD), alpha-synuclein (AS) accumulation is found not only in the brain but also in peripheral tissues, including the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. While many studies have investigated peripheral AS accumulation as a potential in vivo pathological biomarker for PD, data regarding early-onset PD and parkinsonism remain scarce. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate AS accumulation in the GI tract of patients with early-onset parkinsonism. METHODS: Patients with early-onset parkinsonism (age at onset ≤ 50 years) who underwent radical GI surgery for cancer were retrospectively identified. For each patient, two full-thickness tissue blocks from histologically normal proximal and distal resection margins were analyzed. Immunohistochemistry was performed using antibodies against phosphorylated AS (pAS) to detect pathological aggregation and neurofilament to confirm neural localization. RESULTS: A total of 10 patients with early-onset parkinsonism were included in the analysis. The mean age at symptom onset was 43.2 ± 6.1 years. GI surgery was performed at a mean of 12.3 ± 9.0 years after disease onset. Genetic testing results were available for four patients (40%). AS accumulation was identified in 6 patients (60%). Notably, one patient confirmed to have a spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 (SCA6) mutation also exhibited AS accumulation in the stomach. CONCLUSIONS: GI AS accumulation was observed in a substantial proportion of patients with early-onset parkinsonism. Furthermore, its presence in SCA6-related parkinsonism warrants further investigation of peripheral synuclein pathology in genetic parkinsonian disorders.

papers.title: Proceedings of the 7th world Parkinson congress.
Qualitative analysis of staff views on caring for inpatients with delirium and Parkinson's disease: Challenges, tensions and team working.
papers.abstract: ObjectivesPeople with Parkinson's disease (PD) are at increased risk of delirium. Documentation of delirium is poor, with challenges in making a diagnosis due to overlapping symptoms. This study interviewed healthcare workers about their experiences of caring for inpatients with PD and delirium to explore their perspectives.DesignA qualitative study with semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis.ParticipantsTwelve healthcare staff, comprising five doctors and seven nurses.ResultsFour themes emerged: environmental pressures, relationship tensions, challenges and team working. We divided findings into those relevant to all inpatients with delirium and those specific to patients with PD and delirium. Environment pressures negatively impacted on all patients with delirium, and empathy was expressed for all carers/relatives. Staff anxiety was higher caring for patients with PD and relationship tensions occurred with juxtaposition of staff delirium expertise and patient/carer lived experience of PD. PD specific challenges were PD medications and a reciprocal relationship between diagnostic overshadowing and identifying the cause of delirium. Roles of ward nursing team to identify acute changes and doctors to identify and diagnose delirium in all patients was clearly defined.ConclusionsThis study identified knowledge gaps and lack of confidence specific to patients with delirium and PD. We recommend clearer definition of delirium superimposed on PD, with education and training on its complexity, alongside inclusion of expert-by-experience teaching. Future study of patient and carer views will help better understand the relationship tensions and how we can improve patient care and experiences.

papers.title: Research on dynamic functional connectivity and graph theoretic features of different motor subtypes in Parkinson's disease based on ICA.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study combined independent component analysis (ICA)-derived dynamic functional connectivity (dFNC) with dynamic graph theory analysis methods to analyze the changes in dFNC and dynamic graph theoretic indicators in different motor subtypes of Parkinson's disease (PD)-tremor-dominant (TD) subtype and postural instability/gait difficulty (PIGD) subtype-and healthy controls (HC). We aimed to explore the neural circuitry abnormal mechanisms and differences between the two subtypes. METHODS: Using a prospective observational study design, from January 2021 to May 2024 at Northern Jiangsu People's Hospital, we enrolled 36 diagnosed PD patients according to inclusion criteria-19 patients with PIGD subtype and 17 patients with TD subtype-along with 19 healthy subjects matched for age, sex, and education level. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI), demographic information, and clinical motor function assessment data were collected from all participants. The ICA and dynamic functional network connectivity (dFNC) analysis were performed using the GIFT toolbox platform based on MATLAB. Combined with dynamic graph theory analysis, features such as characteristic path length, clustering coefficient, and node degree were extracted. The dFNC and dynamic graph theoretic indicators of the PIGD group, TD group, and HC group were compared horizontally to clarify the common and specific dynamic abnormalities of brain networks between the two subtypes. RESULTS: Nine functional brain networks were identified through ICA. Significant differences among the three groups were observed in five brain networks: auditory network, left frontoparietal network, right frontoparietal network, ventral attention network, and sensorimotor network. papers.title: Dibucaine induces autophagic flux and reduces Ser129-phosphorylated α-synuclein in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons with SNCA duplication.
papers.abstract: The accumulation of α-synuclein (α-syn) in the form of Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites is a neuropathological hallmark of Parkinson's disease (PD) and is closely associated with disease progression. Targeting the autophagy pathway to enhance the clearance of α-syn aggregates therefore represents a promising therapeutic strategy. In the present study, we conducted high-throughput screening using rat embryonic primary neurons, followed by validation of the identified compounds in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons. We identified dibucaine, a local anesthetic, as a compound that induced autophagic flux in neuronal models. In human iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons from a patient with PD carrying an SNCA

papers.title: Digital health meets Parkinson's disease: a bibliometric exploration of wearable sensors research and emerging frontiers (2005-2026).
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Wearable and sensor-based monitoring technologies are increasingly used to support objective, longitudinal assessment in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, the global development, knowledge structure, and emerging research frontiers of this interdisciplinary field remain incompletely mapped. METHODS: Bibliographic records on wearable and sensor-based monitoring technologies in PD were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and Scopus for the period from 1 January 2005 to 2 February 2026. Searches were conducted in title, abstract, and author keyword fields. Microsoft Excel, VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and the bibliometrix R package were used to analyze publication trends, collaboration networks, co-citation patterns, keyword co-occurrence, clustering, citation bursts, historiographic patterns, and source impact. RESULTS: A total of 3,332 publications were included. Publication output increased rapidly over the study period, particularly after 2019, while 2026 represented an incomplete publication year because the search was conducted on 2 February 2026. The United States (U.S.), China, and European countries constituted the main knowledge-production and collaboration structure. Thematic analyses suggested a gradual shift from engineering validation and objective motor-symptom quantification toward AI-enabled digital biomarkers, remote monitoring, multimodal monitoring, and closed-loop neuromodulation. These patterns reflect research activity and citation structures rather than direct evidence of clinical efficacy. CONCLUSION: This bibliometric analysis provides science-mapping evidence on the evolution of wearable and sensor-based monitoring technologies in PD. Future work should prioritize standardization, multicenter real-world validation, clinical workflow integration, multimodal data fusion, and cautious evaluation of closed-loop applications.

papers.title: Tegmental atrophy in isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder: ex vivo MRI-informed in vivo imaging.
papers.abstract: Isolated rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder (iRBD) is an early-stage synucleinopathy characterized by brainstem pathology. In rodents, the pontine tegmentum contains a REM sleep centre, the sublaterodorsal nucleus, which expresses corticotropin-releasing hormone binding protein (CRHBP). While the involvement of brainstem pathophysiology is thus implicated in iRBD, its solid evidence remains scarce in humans due to the difficulty in identifying small brainstem nuclei with conventional MRI technology alone. Here, we aimed to detect tegmental atrophy in iRBD with voxel-based morphometry (VBM) analysis combined with a novel human brainstem atlas. Structural MRIs from 98 patients with iRBD and 114 controls were analysed to investigate grey matter volume using VBM. Our unique approach involved detailed assessments of the VBM results, guided by a high-resolution MRI-based atlas of the human brainstem. This brainstem atlas was founded on ex vivo

papers.title: Gut-Derived α-Synuclein Condensates in Parkinson's Disease: Linking Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation, Blood Dissemination, and Chemical Biology.
papers.abstract: Two advances have reshaped our understanding of α-synuclein (αSyn) in Parkinson's disease (PD). First, αSyn can assemble through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and related condensation pathways, forming condensates that mature into Lewy-body-like assemblies. Although conventional crowding-driven LLPS requires supraphysiological protein concentrations, membrane-templated surface condensation has been reported in vitro at ~10 nM, making this pathway plausible in the lipid-rich, electrically active enteric nervous system (ENS). Second, seeding-competent αSyn is detectable in blood before motor onset using seed-amplification assays. This review asks whether condensate-derived αSyn generated in the gut constitutes a blood-borne seed population that is systematically underrepresented by fibril-biased assays. We evaluate each step of the proposed pathway, including gut-specific LLPS triggers, release into and survival within the circulation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) traversal, and clinical detection, while distinguishing established evidence from indirect inference and testable hypotheses. Many of these questions are now experimentally accessible. Molecular rotors detect condensates through microviscosity rather than cross-β structure, condensate-stage modulators have emerged, and receptor-interception strategies such as bemcentinib provide opportunities for mechanistic interrogation. Together, these advances position chemical biology to determine whether condensate-derived seeds contribute to PD pathogenesis.

papers.title: Subject-independent Parkinson's Disease Detection through A Lightweight Spectrotemporal Hybrid Network.
papers.journal: Journal of medical signals and sensors
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Vocal impairment constitutes a prominent prodromal biomarker for Parkinson's disease (PD). However, existing deep learning solutions often rely on computationally intensive architectures or biased validation protocols. This study proposes the lightweight spectrotemporal hybrid network (LST-Net), a resource-efficient framework for robust PD screening. METHODS: The model employs a dual-stream architecture that concurrently processes raw one-dimensional waveforms and two-dimensional Mel-spectrograms to capture complementary cues, specifically transient temporal jitters and spectral energy patterns. The proposed architecture was evaluated on the Italian Parkinson's Voice and Speech dataset using a strict subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation protocol to prevent data leakage. RESULTS: The proposed LST-Net achieved a robust segment-level accuracy of 96.69%. By implementing a subject-level majority voting strategy, mimicking clinical diagnosis where patients are assessed over time, the model successfully classified all subjects in the held-out test sets (100% subject-level accuracy). Quantitative Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping analysis confirmed the model's focus on clinically relevant low-frequency tremors (mean energy: 61.56% ±27.90%). CONCLUSIONS: This framework demonstrates that explicit spectrotemporal fusion yields superior diagnostic performance without heavy computational burdens, offering a verifiable and scalable solution for real-time deployment on edge devices.

papers.title: PET-based molecular imaging in neurodegeneration and dementia: current and emerging radiotracers.
papers.abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET)-based molecular imaging is a clinically important tool for the evaluation of dementia and other neurodegenerative disorders, using radiotracers that target specific molecular and pathophysiological processes. Fluorodeoxyglucose brain PET has historically supported neurodegenerative disorder evaluation through detection of characteristic patterns of regional glucose hypometabolism. In recent years, the molecular imaging of protein aggregates has taken on an increasingly important role. This is evident with the widespread clinical adoption of amyloid PET and early use of tau PET to provide diagnostic and prognostic information for patients with suspected Alzheimer's disease. Additional classes of radiotracers relevant to neurodegenerative diseases are under active investigation, including those targeting neuroinflammation, synaptic density, and α-synuclein aggregates. We review the major classes of PET radiotracers for neurodegenerative diseases, describing their molecular mechanisms, diagnostic performance, and their current and emerging clinical roles in dementia evaluation. Case examples for clinically used tracers illustrate imaging features relevant to diagnosis and characterization of prognosis and treatment effect. Finally, we discuss early developments and current challenges in the development of theranostic approaches and novel radiotracers for neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Vascularizing neurospheroids to probe vascular contributions to α-synuclein pathology in Parkinson's disease.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are increasingly associated with vascular dysfunction beyond progressive neuronal degeneration, yet how vascular pathology contributes to disease progression remains poorly understood, largely due to the lack of a neurodegenerative disease model capable of capturing neuronal pathology alongside associated vascular dysfunction. Here, we developed a microengineered 3D vascularized brain tissue model that integrates neurospheroids with a self-assembled, perfusable vascular network to recapitulate key features of the neurovascular interface. Using this model, we investigated the vascular contribution to Parkinson's disease pathology by introducing α-synuclein preformed fibrils into the engineered vasculature. Intravascular α-syn fibril exposure induced endothelial barrier disruption, vascular leakage, inflammation, and vascular regression. Notably, this vascular insult was accompanied by intraneuronal α-synuclein aggregation within neurospheroids, suggesting that vascular dysfunction may facilitate the exposure of neural tissue to pathogenic α-synuclein. Our neurodegenerative disease modeling approach establishes a versatile and tractable platform for investigating vascular contributions to neurodegenerative disease progression.

papers.title: α-Synuclein Seeding Activity in Fixed Antemortem Skin Biopsies From Patients With Synucleinopathies.
papers.abstract: α-Synuclein seed amplification assays can detect seed-competent pathological α-synuclein in fresh and frozen biospecimens, but their performance in fixed antemortem skin biopsies is less well defined. We applied an optimized real-time quaking-induced conversion assay to paraformaldehyde-fixed skin biopsy sections from participants with Parkinson's disease (PD), dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), multiple system atrophy (MSA), and controls. Fixed tissue retained measurable α-synuclein seeding activity, although amplification was delayed and the apparent 50% seeding dose was lower than in unfixed or autopsy skin. In this selected proof-of-concept cohort, SAA positivity was observed in 70% of PD, 80% of DLB, 80% of MSA, and 20% of control samples; exploratory ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.86. Seeding readouts correlated with Hoehn and Yahr stage but not significantly with MoCA score or pS129 α-synuclein burden. Fixed skin biopsies can therefore provide complementary morphological and functional measures of peripheral α-synuclein pathology.

papers.title: Iron-related biomarkers and Lewy body dementia: a scoping review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Iron dysregulation is implicated in neurodegenerative disease pathophysiology, but its role in Lewy body dementia (LBD) remains poorly characterized. This review mapped iron-related measures across blood, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and brain compartments and evaluate their potential relevance as biomarkers in LBD. METHODS: A scoping review was conducted according to PRISMA-ScR guidelines using PubMed and Web of Science. Studies reporting iron-related biomarkers in individuals with LBD were eligible regardless of biological compartment; review articles and non-LBD studies were excluded. Of 222 identified records, 24 met inclusion criteria. Data were charted using a standardized extraction framework and due to methodological heterogeneity, were synthesized qualitatively across blood and CSF measures, postmortem brain analyses, and in vivo RESULTS: Brain-based measures showed the most consistent iron-related alterations, particularly quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM), with abnormalities across cortical, limbic, and subcortical regions, although findings were not universal. Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) provided complementary evidence of nigrosome-1 abnormalities. Peripheral and CSF measures were heterogeneous and showed no consistent directional pattern. No study directly compared measures across all three compartments within the same cohort. CONCLUSION: Iron dysregulation in LBD appears more pronounced in brain than systemic compartments, though within-cohort cross-compartment comparisons are lacking. Brain iron accumulation extends beyond the substantia nigra, aligning with Lewy body pathology and potentially explaining LBD's distinctive cognitive and neuropsychiatric features. QSM and SWI are promising candidate imaging biomarkers, though current evidence reflects group-level differences rather than individual-patient diagnostic accuracy. Longitudinal, cross-compartment studies are needed to clarify their clinical significance in

papers.title: Hyperexcitable primary somatosensory cortex in the MitoPark mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: UNLABELLED: The majority of Parkinson's disease patients suffer from decreased tactile acuity or neuropathic pain, both of which contribute to low quality of life and likely exacerbate motor dysfunction. How Parkinson's disease pathology relates to altered somatosensation remains unclear. One potential contributor is the progressive degeneration of dopamine neurons. To assess the extent to which gradual dopamine neuron loss contributes to altered somatosensation, we recorded spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity in the primary somatosensory cortex of the MitoPark mouse model of Parkinson's disease. MitoPark mice experience progressive dopamine neuron degeneration that is independent of α-synuclein. We found that MitoPark layer V regular-spiking (largely pyramidal) neurons, but not fast-spiking (largely parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory) neurons, had elevated spontaneous firing rates relative to littermate controls at late stages of symptom progression. Regular-spiking neurons also became hyperresponsive to tactile stimuli - more neurons were recruited by stimuli across a wide range of intensities, and these neurons responded with higher firing rates. Fast-spiking neurons, but not regular-spiking neurons, became desynchronized at late stages of symptom progression. These physiological changes coincided with pronounced degeneration of dopamine neurons and axons, which we measured with tyrosine hydroxylase immunostaining in the midbrain, striatum, and primary somatosensory cortex. Altogether, this characterization revealed cell-type-specific changes in the primary somatosensory cortex that are consistent with both decreased tactile acuity and hyperalgesia in Parkinson's disease patients. This suggests that the loss of dopamine neurons, potentially including those that innervate primary somatosensory cortex, contributes to somatosensory impairments associated with Parkinson's disease. papers.title: Photobiomodulation in Parkinson's disease: From pathogenesis to intervention.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder clinically characterized by bradykinesia, rest tremor, rigidity, and postural instability. Its core pathological features include the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons within the substantia nigra pars compacta, striatal dopamine depletion, and intracellular accumulation of misfolded α-Synuclein (α-Syn)-rich Lewy inclusions that trigger neuronal dysfunction and cell death. Despite substantial research efforts, existing pharmacological strategies targeting α-Syn and dopaminergic neurons show limited capacity to halt or reverse PD progression, creating an urgent need for novel alternative therapeutic interventions. Photobiomodulation (PBM) is a non-invasive phototherapy that delivers photonic energy to biological tissues using visible and near-infrared light. Preclinical studies have documented neuroprotective signals linked to PBM in experimental PD models; however, clinical studies to date provide only preliminary and inconsistent evidence regarding safety and possible symptomatic benefit. This narrative review outlines the mechanistic rationale, preclinical findings, clinical observations, and key translational limitations for PBM as an investigational adjunctive intervention in PD. We first elaborate on PD-related pathological mechanisms, followed by an in-depth discussion of PBM-mediated biological actions, and consolidate recent evidence for its anti-PD applications in preclinical settings. Available preclinical data suggest PBM could modulate mitochondrial function, neuroinflammation, dopaminergic-neuron survival, and responses along the microbiota-gut-brain axis in experimental PD models, though direct evidence supporting modification of α-synuclein aggregation or propagation remains sparse. Clinical observations support procedural feasibility and acceptable short-term safety profiles. Nevertheless, definitive clinical efficacy cannot be confirmed given small sam

papers.title: Human DOPA Decarboxylase in Monoamine Metabolism, Pharmacology, and Synucleinopathies.
papers.abstract: Human DOPA decarboxylase is the pyridoxal 5'-phosphate-dependent enzyme that produces dopamine and serotonin. For most of its history it has been treated as a constitutive downstream step rather than a point of regulation, and it has received correspondingly little mechanistic attention. The human enzyme is broadly expressed across central monoaminergic neurons and peripheral neuroendocrine tissues, where it operates in different chemical environments and under different pharmacological constraints. Structurally, it interconverts between an open, cofactor-free apo-form and a closed, catalytically competent holo-form, with conformational dynamics that extend well beyond the active site. Its activity is further tuned by cofactor availability, by phosphorylation, and by protein partners, of which the most notable is α-synuclein Its effect on the enzyme is documented in cellular systems but still unresolved at the molecular level. Pharmacologically, carbidopa is its principal peripheral inhibitor, but its mechanism remains incompletely characterized, and chronic therapy raises rather than lowers circulating AADC levels. In parallel, AADC measured in cerebrospinal fluid has emerged as one of the most discriminating fluid biomarkers for Parkinson's disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, with changes detectable years before motor onset. These different layers, structural, regulatory, pharmacological, and diagnostic, converge on a single enzyme whose biology has long been treated as settled, and which is now being reevaluated as a fundamental node in the molecular landscape of synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Twenty-five years of progress in Parkinson's disease research: from dopamine replacement to biological definition and regenerative therapy.
papers.abstract: The first quarter of the twenty-first century has transformed Parkinson's disease (PD) from a predominantly motor, dopamine-deficiency syndrome into a heterogeneous multisystem disorder defined across clinical, genetic and molecular dimensions. This overview follows the trajectory of these advances from the historical foundations established prior 2000 to present concepts of prodromal disease, progression, biological classification and precision medicine. Epidemiological work has established PD as the fastest-growing major neurological disorder, while systematic characterization of non-motor symptoms has shifted diagnosis and attention beyond the nigrostriatal system in PD research. Imaging has progressed from exclusionary structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to quantitative susceptibility, diffusion and molecular approaches, although no single imaging biomarker yet provides a stand-alone diagnosis of PD. The discovery of α-synuclein gene mutations and its presence as protein in Lewy bodies and neurites connected genetics, protein aggregation and selective neuronal vulnerability. Seed amplification assays (SAA) now enable robust detection of pathological α-synuclein in cerebrospinal fluid and have catalysed biologically anchored staging proposals. At the same time, negative phase 2 antibody against α-synuclein trials illustrate the challenges of target engagement, disease heterogeneity and intervention timing. Genetics and cell biology have placed lysosomal proteostasis, in particular glucocerebrosidase 1 (GBA1) dependent pathways, at the center of disease-modification strategies. Dopaminergic therapy remains extraordinarily effective symptomatically, with continuous delivery systems extending its utility for intermediate and late stages of the disease, whereas cell replacement has re-entered clinical development through standardized pluripotent-stem-cell-derived midbrain dopaminergic progenitors. papers.title: Leveraging the Gut Microbiota for Mechanistically Informed Therapeutics against Body-First Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: Although some symptoms of Parkinson's disease can be pharmacologically alleviated, stopping disease progression is not currently possible. Motor impairment in Parkinson's disease is associated with accumulation of aggregates of the protein α-synuclein (α-syn) in dopaminergic neurons in the brain. In some Parkinson's disease cases, these pathogenic aggregates accumulate in the intestinal lining years before motor symptoms manifest. This long prodromal period provides a window of opportunity to detect Parkinson's disease and halt its progression. Specifically, elucidating the factors involved in disease onset in the gut would enable prevention of α-syn aggregation before it spreads to the brain. In this perspective, we highlight discoveries of gut bacteria that induce aggregation of intestinal α-syn as well as efforts to decipher the molecular-level mechanisms by which this process occurs. We also showcase the rationale and potential breadth of applications focused on manipulating the gut microbiome, including biotics, fecal microbiome transplants, and microbial editing. By understanding molecular mechanisms of intestinal α-syn aggregation, the microbiome may be harnessed to control the factors responsible for their pathogenic formation and spread. Such insights will ultimately enable the development of more effective therapeutics for prevention and treatment of Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: Biological functions of progranulin and research progress in neurodegenerative diseases.
papers.abstract: Progranulin (PGRN), a multifunctional glycoprotein, is widely expressed in the central nervous system, particularly in microglia. Dysregulation of PGRN is strongly linked to the pathogenesis of frontotemporal dementia (FTD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), and Parkinson's disease (PD), highlighting its essential role in brain homeostasis. While there are several mechanisms through which PGRN regulates lysosomal function, lipid metabolism, neuroinflammation, and microglial activation have been elucidated, its precise pathological network in neurodegenerative diseases remains incompletely understood. This review summarizes the biological functions of PGRN and recent research progress in neurodegenerative diseases, and discusses its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target. In addition, we propose an integrative "cascade-amplifying pathological network" hypothesis - a self-reinforcing positive feedback loop involving lysosomal dysfunction, lipid accumulation, and microglial activation, with the strongest evidence in GRN-mutation FTD and emerging relevance to AD and PD. Moreover, we incorporate recent advances from 2024-2026, including updated clinical trial outcomes, novel insights into PGRN-mediated lipid metabolism regulation, and emerging evidence on cell-type-specific mechanisms of PGRN function.

papers.title: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells: Context-Dependent resilience and vulnerability.
papers.journal: Neurobiology of sleep and circadian rhythms
papers.abstract: Retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) exhibit marked heterogeneity in their susceptibility to injury and disease. Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), a small subset of melanopsin-expressing RGCs involved in non-image-forming visual functions, have emerged as a particularly informative example. In multiple experimental models, ipRGCs show relative resistance to acute insults such as optic nerve injury, excitotoxicity, and mitochondrial dysfuinction. In contrast, functional alterations and degeneration have been reported in aging and in neurodegenerative conditions including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. This apparent discrepancy suggests that ipRGC survival may depend on the nature and duration of the underlying stress. In this review, we summarize current evidence on ipRGC resilience and vulnerability across a range of experimental and pathological contexts. We discuss candidate mechanisms that may contribute to these responses, including sustained activity, calcium handling, metabolic specialization, neurochemical interactions, and gene expression programs. We also consider the role of subtype-specific diversity within the ipRGC population in shaping these outcomes. Finally, we examine the potential of ipRGCs as biomarkers of disease and as a source of insight for neuroprotective strategies. Together, these observations support the view that ipRGC behaviour reflects an interaction between intrinsic cellular properties and the context in which they are engaged.

papers.title: Spatially Resolved Multiplex Detection of Cytokines in Parkinson's Disease Rat Brain via CRISPR/Cas Biosensing.
papers.abstract: The ability to accurately quantify localized neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative biomarkers in vivo is critical for enabling the early diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD). Here, we demonstrate a strategy for localized neuroinflammation quantification using an implantable glass-fiber-based CRISPR/Cas immunosensor. When interfaced with a portable fluorescence detector, our platform enables the spatially resolved multiplex detection of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and alpha-synuclein (α-syn) in the PD rat brain. The sensor surface was modified with functionalized liquid metal nanoparticles to enable antibody immobilization and long-term in vivo operation. This method demonstrated high specificity, excellent linearity in artificial cerebrospinal fluid (R2 > 0.91), sustained surface stability over 28 days, good biocompatibility with PC12 cells, and selective antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus. Following cannula implantation into the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) of a 6-hydroxydopamine-induced PD rat model, the functionalized glass fiber enabled repeated, minimally invasive biomarker sampling at 6, 12, and 24 h postimplantation. Systemic inflammation induced by lipopolysaccharide (LPS) triggered marked elevations in TNF-α, IL-6, and α-syn, peaking at 6 h post-LPS. This implantable fiber-based biosensing method offers a promising reliable approach for early PD diagnosis, disease progression tracking, and investigation of neuroimmune interactions in neurodegenerative diseases in a point-of-care scenario.

papers.title: Wearable sensor-derived gait signatures for Parkinson's disease: an exploratory diagnostic study integrating dimensionality reduction and machine learning.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by progressive motor dysfunction, in which gait disturbances often emerge early yet remain underutilized in diagnostic frameworks. Advances in wearable sensor technology enable high-resolution quantification of gait dynamics, but the clinical translation of such high-dimensional data is limited by redundancy and model overfitting. OBJECTIVE: To determine the exploratory diagnostic efficacy of synthesizing wearable sensor-derived gait parameters, cognitive scores, and blood biomarkers utilizing a dual-stage dimensionality reduction framework coupled with logistic regression machine learning for the precise identification of PD. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, demographic characteristics, blood biomarkers, cognitive assessments, and wearable sensor-derived gait parameters were collected from patients with PD and matched controls. Following initial group comparisons, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was applied to identify candidate predictors from multimodal variables. Principal component analysis (PCA) was subsequently performed to reduce dimensionality and extract latent structures. Logistic regression models were constructed using both the original LASSO-selected variables and PCA-derived components. Model performance was assessed using 10-fold cross-validation, with discrimination quantified by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and accuracy. RESULTS: Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups except for age. LASSO identified 22 potential predictors spanning demographic, biochemical, cognitive, and gait domains. PCA further condensed these variables into six principal components, explaining 62.983% of the total variance. Using a rigorous nested cross-validation framework on the primary cohort, the PCA-based model achieved an internal mean AUC of 0.949 with an accuracy of 0.827. papers.title: Psychotic symptoms in tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency-associated dopa-responsive dystonia treated with antipsychotics and rTMS: a case report.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tyrosine hydroxylase deficiency (THD) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the TH CASE SUMMARY: This report describes a genetically confirmed woman with THD who presented with infantile-onset dystonia. Auditory hallucinations and erotomanic delusions emerged approximately five years after levodopa initiation and persisted despite one-month levodopa withdrawal. Although levodopa markedly improved her dystonia, antipsychotic treatment posed a therapeutic dilemma: risperidone exacerbated motor symptoms, and aripiprazole was limited by poor adherence. A multimodal regimen comprising aripiprazole, quetiapine, and low-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) targeting the left temporoparietal cortex was associated with progressive improvement of psychotic symptoms without clinically apparent worsening of dystonia. The independent contribution of rTMS could not be determined given the concurrent pharmacological titration. CONCLUSION: Selecting appropriate antipsychotic medication in THD patients with prominent psychotic symptoms poses a considerable challenge. The combination of aripiprazole, quetiapine, and rTMS may represent a potential therapeutic option. To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of genetically confirmed DRD due to THD presenting with prominent psychotic symptoms, and among the few documenting rTMS use in this population. These observations are based on clinical assessment without standardized quantitative measures; the independent efficacy of rTMS cannot be established from this case.

papers.title: Effects of hyperbaric oxygen therapy in the treatment of selected diseases of the nervous system.
papers.abstract: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy (HBOT) has attracted increasing interest as a potential supportive intervention in neurological disorders. By increasing the amount of oxygen dissolved in blood plasma, HBOT enhances oxygen delivery to hypoxic tissues and may influence mechanisms involved in neuroplasticity, inflammation, and tissue repair. Experimental and clinical studies suggest that HBOT may support neurological recovery in selected conditions, particularly following ischemic or traumatic brain injury. However, the effectiveness of HBOT varies depending on the underlying disease, and further high-quality clinical studies are needed to establish its role in neurological rehabilitation.The article was based on an analysis of data from Google Scholar and PubMed regarding the effects of hyperbaric therapy.

papers.title: Smartphone placement recognition during walking: External validation and performance determinants.
papers.abstract: The opportunity to collect movement data from smartphones for prolonged periods has opened new perspectives in the field of clinical movement analysis. However, when monitoring people's mobility in free-living conditions, smartphone placement can influence the validity of the extracted digital mobility outcome. This study aimed to develop and validate an automatic smartphone placement recognition classifier and to investigate potential critical factors that can influence performance. The classifier was trained on data from 15 healthy participants using inertial signals collected from smartphones placed at six body placements during free-living walking and externally validated on over 3000 individuals from external datasets, including blind participants and patients with cardiovascular or Parkinson's disease. A decision-tree ensemble model was developed using feature subsets of increasing dimensionality, with the optimal subset comprising 50 features. Classification accuracy increased consistently when front and back pocket placements were aggregated (81.1%) and further improved when coat pocket was also included in the pocket class (88.5%), underscoring the challenge of distinguishing between fine-grained pocket placements. The best-recognised placements across the external datasets were lower back (precision: 100%, recall: 72.5%), hand (precision: 94.2%, recall: 94.5%), and the aggregated pocket class (precision: 86.7%, recall: 90.2%). Recognition accuracy changed across cohorts (0.73 - 0.85), activities (0.63 - 0.94) and speed (0.79 - 0.87), however it stayed consistent across various technological and environmental factors. Overall, this study supports the feasibility of smartphone placement recognition in walking and underscores the importance of accounting for key influencing factors when designing frameworks intended for deployment in heterogeneous real-world or clinical contexts.

papers.title: Frontal stimulation reshapes SCAN connectivity and improves motor function in Parkinson's disease.
papers.journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder with characteristic motor deficits of bradykinesia and impaired coordination, and non-motor deficits affecting cognitive abilities such as attention and executive functions. Recent evidence suggests that some canonical motor deficits in Parkinson's disease (e.g., freezing of gait) are associated with abnormalities in frontal cortical processing typically thought to underlie executive functions such as cognitive control. The evidence from human research linking frontal cognitive disruption and motor deficits in people with Parkinson's disease is correlational. Individuals with cognitive impairments often also display gait and balance deficits, but causal evidence remains lacking. We combined non-invasive brain stimulation with functional MRI (fMRI) to ascertain whether dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) exerts a causal influence modulating motor function and to test the hypothesis that an excitatory stimulation protocol applied to a cognitive control network can improve motor performance in Parkinson disease. Participants with Parkinson's disease performed a precision force-tracking task shown to track with gait impairment while undergoing functional neuroimaging scans. On half of trials, participants were required to simultaneously perform a cognitively demanding 2-back working memory task to tax attentional systems. Following the initial baseline scan, participants returned for three separate counterbalanced sessions that combined transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in the form of theta burst stimulation (TBS) with fMRI. Just prior to task performance, participants received either excitatory (intermittent TBS) or inhibitory (continuous TBS) stimulation protocols over right DLPFC. In the third session, participants received stimulation to a control site outside the cognitive and motor areas implicated in our task. Our within-subjects experimental design allowed us to examine the effects of stimulation on mo

papers.title: Argentine Tango as an Integrative Therapeutic Approach: Bridging Dance Therapy and Melotherapy.
papers.journal: Journal of functional morphology and kinesiology
papers.abstract: Argentine tango integrates rhythmic auditory information, adaptive locomotion, improvisation, and continuous partnered interaction within a complex dance practice. This review examines its therapeutic relevance with primary emphasis on neurological rehabilitation, particularly Parkinson's disease (PD), where tango-specific evidence is most developed. Particular attention is given to balance, functional mobility, gait adaptability, and motor-cognitive integration, while cognitive, emotional, and social outcomes are considered complementary dimensions rather than equivalent primary endpoints. This review examines mechanisms involving auditory-motor coupling, motor learning, embodied cognition, and interpersonal coordination, while distinguishing tango-based interventions from formal dance/movement therapy and music therapy. Particular consideration is given to Adapted Tango, including how task demands can be scaled while preserving defining characteristics of Argentine tango. Rather than claiming superiority over other dance forms, the review proposes that tango is therapeutically relevant because of its distinctive combination of walking-based multidirectional locomotion, musical interpretation, improvisational decision-making, and partner-derived sensory information. These relationships are integrated within the Argentine Tango Therapeutic Integration Model (ATTIM), proposed as a hypothesis-generating framework for future research.

papers.title: Rapidly Progressive Dementia and Parkinsonism Secondary to Intracranial Dural Arteriovenous Fistula in a 60-year-old Male: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Simultaneous rapidly progressive dementia with parkinsonism is a rare initial presentation of dural arteriovenous fistula. Most cases of dural arteriovenous fistula present with either sudden-onset headache and cerebrovascular disease hemorrhage or other benign non-hemorrhagic symptoms. We present a unique case of a 60-year-old male who presented with progressive slowness of movement and forgetfulness. Physical examination was initially significant for bradykinetic movements, slowed gait, and reduced arm swing bilaterally, along with a MoCA score of 15/30, indicating moderate cognitive impairment. Cerebral catheter angiography revealed the presence of a complex tentorial-torcular-left transverse sinus-sigmoid sinus dural arteriovenous fistula. A month after the diagnosis, he eventually became stuporous and bedbound, with episodes of generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and was thus given Levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. The patient underwent partial arterial feeder onyx embolization with a transverse approach. He was admitted to intensive care post-operatively, with gradual improvement of stupor and no seizure recurrence thereafter. Upon discharge, he was maintained on Memantine, slowly increased to 10 mg twice daily. Seven months after embolization, the patient ambulated without assistance. Although bradykinesia and dementia were still present, this represented a significant improvement from the condition pre-embolization. A high index of suspicion and awareness of this rare acquired cause of rapidly progressive dementia and parkinsonism is needed to avoid delays in the diagnosis and appropriate management.

papers.title: Sleep and the Gut-Brain Axis: Bidirectional, Converging Mechanisms Linking Brain Health, Neuroinflammation, and Neurodegeneration.
papers.journal: Pathophysiology : the official journal of the International Society for Pathophysiology
papers.abstract: Sleep and the gastrointestinal (GI) tract interact in a complex and reciprocal relationship, although the molecular and physiological pathways underlying this interaction remain only partially defined. Communication between the central (CNS) and enteric nervous systems (ENS) spans neural, immune, endocrine, and metabolic pathways, including vagal nerve signaling, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, gut-resident microbiota, and circulating microbial metabolites, such as bile acids with neuroinflammatory or neurotransmitter activity. In this narrative review, we synthesize evidence from animal models, observational cohorts, and intervention trials to map this bidirectional axis, focusing on several underexamined modulatory mechanisms including the interaction between the gut microbiome and the glymphatic system, the brain's perivascular waste-clearance network, which is implicated in the removal of amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau in Alzheimer's disease; neuroendocrine regulation and sex-related differences in gut microbiome composition and sleep patterns, which may help explain the divergent neurodegenerative disease risks between men and women; and age-related parallel trajectories of microbiome senescence and sleep fragmentation in older adults. We discuss melatonin, cortisol, estrogen, and ghrelin as endocrine mediators linking circadian biology to gut physiology, and we consider how environmental and lifestyle factors further perturb this system. These mechanisms form an integrative framework of the gut-brain-sleep axis and highlight priority directions for mechanistic and translational research, including significant nodes in this pathway where targeted interventions may help cognitive resilience and slow the neurodegenerative disease progression. More research clarifying these mechanisms may help identify the most promising targets, potentially leading to personalized, precision-medicine-based therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: RGS10 controls the metabolic and neuroinflammatory benefits of NLRP3 suppression in diet-induced obesity in male mice.
papers.abstract: The NLRP3 inflammasome is a central mediator of metabolic inflammation, yet the upstream mechanisms remain poorly defined. We identified RGS10 as a critical regulator of NLRP3-driven immunometabolic responses. In macrophages, loss of RGS10 enhanced calcium-dependent NLRP3 inflammasome activity during both priming and activation. In high-fat diet-fed male mice, Nlrp3 deletion improved glucose tolerance, adipose remodeling, and hepatic and hypothalamic pathology, whereas Rgs10 deletion induced the opposite phenotype. These benefits required RGS10: in Nlrp3 -/-/

papers.title: Changes in sleep disturbances and quality of life associated with Istradefylline in patients with Parkinson's disease: an exploratory polysomnographic study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sleep disturbances are common non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD) and substantially impair quality of life (QOL). Although istradefylline, an adenosine A2A receptor antagonist, is widely used to improve motor fluctuations, its effects on subjective sleep complaints and objective sleep architecture remain unclear. METHODS: In this exploratory, single-center, open-label study, we evaluated changes in subjective sleep quality and polysomnographic findings following 12 weeks of istradefylline treatment in patients with PD. Nine patients underwent clinical assessments and overnight polysomnography at baseline and 12 weeks after initiating istradefylline (20 mg/day). Sleep quality, QOL, fatigue, and motor symptoms were assessed using validated clinical scales. RESULTS: Following istradefylline initiation, improvements were observed in Parkinson's Disease Sleep Scale-2 (PDSS-2), Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 summary index (PDQ-39 SI), Parkinson Fatigue Scale, and Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part IV scores. Changes in PDSS-2 scores were significantly correlated with changes in PDQ-39 SI (ρ = 0.76, p CONCLUSIONS: In this small uncontrolled study, initiation of istradefylline was associated with improvements in subjective sleep quality, fatigue, and QOL, whereas objective polysomnographic parameters showed limited changes. These findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger controlled studies.

papers.title: Effects of butylphthalide plus donepezil on symptoms, cognitive function, and oxidative stress in patients with cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the effects of butylphthalide combined with donepezil on clinical symptoms, cognitive function, and oxidative stress in patients with cognitive impairment associated with Parkinson's disease (PD). METHODS: A total of 119 patients with PD-associated cognitive impairment who were admitted to Chengdu Sixth People's Hospital (Donghong Branch) were retrospectively included and divided into two groups. Both groups received levodopa and benserazide hydrochloride as basic treatment. In addition, patients in the control group (n = 55) received donepezil, and those in the research group (n = 64) received butylphthalide combined with donepezil. The two groups were compared in terms of therapeutic efficacy, clinical symptoms (assessed by the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale [UPDRS]), cognitive function (Montreal Cognitive Assessment [MoCA]), activities of daily living (ADLs; ADL scale), neurotransmitter levels (dopamine [DA], gamma-aminobutyric acid [GABA], 5-hydroxytryptamine [5-HT]), neurotrophic factors (neurotrophin-3 [NT-3], nerve growth factor [NGF]), oxidative stress (superoxide dismutase [SOD], malondialdehyde [MDA]), adverse events, and quality of life (QoL; the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey [SF-36]). Furthermore, exploratory subgroup analyses were performed according to Hoehn-Yahr staging (H-Y staging) and baseline MoCA scores. RESULTS: Compared to the control group, patients in the research group exhibited much higher overall response rate, lower post-treatment UPDRSII, UPDRSIII, and MDA levels, and higher MoCA scores, ADL scores, DA, GABA, 5-HT, NT-3, NGF, SOD levels, and SF-36 scores. The overall incidence of adverse events was comparable between groups. Neither H-Y staging nor baseline MoCA scores significantly affected the efficacy of the combination therapy. papers.title: The LRRK2 R1441G+M1646T haplotype is associated with slower motor symptom progression in Parkinson's disease.
papers.journal: medRxiv : the preprint server for health sciences
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 ( LRRK2 METHODS: We analyzed up to 12 years of longitudinal data from 603 participants in the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) with PD and available whole-genome sequencing data: 394 sporadic PD, 169 G2019S carriers, 20 R1441G+M1646T carriers, and 20 M1646T carriers. Motor symptom progression (MDS-UPDRS III) was assessed using linear mixed-effects models with genotype-by-time interactions, adjusted for age at onset, disease duration at baseline, sex, race, baseline score, and levodopa equivalent daily dose. RESULTS: R1441G+M1646T carriers exhibited 76% slower progression in OFF-state MDS-UPDRS III than sporadic PD (0.50 vs. 2.04 points/year; β=-1.54 [95% CI: -2.48, -0.60]; p=0.001). G2019S carriers exhibited 26% slower progression (1.52 points/year; β=-0.52 [-0.99, -0.06]; p=0.03). M1646T carriers did not differ from sporadic PD (p=0.60). Slower progression in R1441G+M1646T carriers was characterized by attenuated bradykinesia (64% slower; p=0.008), axial decline (76% slower; p=0.002), and a lack of orofacial symptom progression (p<0.001). R1441G+M1646T carriers also exhibited 55% slower self-reported motor decline (MDS-UPDRS II; p=0.04). CONCLUSIONS: R1441G+M1646T carriers exhibit substantially slower motor progression than sporadic PD while M1646T carriers do not.

papers.title: Single-Nucleus Phosphatome Rewiring and Phosphoproteomics Reveal PFKFB2 as an LRRK2-Linked Metabolic Node in Human Parkinsonian Substantia Nigra.
papers.abstract: Aberrant signaling by leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) drives Parkinson's disease (PD) biology, linking Rab phosphorylation to endolysosomal dysfunction. However, how LRRK2-linked trafficking intersects with metabolic remodeling within vulnerable human substantia nigra cell states remains poorly defined. Here, phosphatome-wide systems analysis, single-nucleus transcriptomics, structural modeling, and independent phosphoproteomic evidence were integrated to identify the glycolytic regulator PFKFB2 as a phosphorylation-associated metabolic node. Sample-level pseudobulk profiling of a human substantia nigra single-nucleus RNA-seq data set revealed distributed phosphatome remodeling across the PD spectrum, prioritizing PFKFB2 as a transcriptionally reduced, dynamically rewired systems hub. Full-atlas analysis across 390,360 nuclei showed that this tissue-level decrease resolved into disease-stage-specific cellular redistribution: PFKFB2 was reduced across oligodendrocyte-lineage and neuronal compartments in PD, whereas Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD) showed microglial induction alongside astrocytic and neuronal loss. Stratification by PFKFB2 expression revealed marked transcriptional polarity: PFKFB2-positive cellular states were enriched for LRRK2-Rab trafficking and lysosomal programs, whereas PFKFB2-negative states retained mitochondrial/OXPHOS signatures; paired donor-pseudobulk analysis confirmed that the principal PFKFB2-associated PDD microglial program was reproducible across donors. Structurally, AlphaFold-guided peptide docking identified the flexible C-terminal regulatory tail of PFKFB2 as a kinase-accessible region, prioritizing the conserved Ser483 locus as the strongest LRRK2-compatible structural candidate. papers.title: Neurodegenerative Diseases: Epidemiology, Risk Factors, Classification, Pathophysiology, Clinical Features, Diagnosis, and Therapeutic Strategies.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are a growing cause of disability worldwide, particularly as populations age. Although these disorders differ in etiology and clinical presentation, advances in genetics, neuropathology, and biomarker research have identified shared disturbances in protein homeostasis, mitochondrial function, and immune regulation. These processes may contribute to selective neuronal vulnerability and neural circuit dysfunction. These findings are refining disease classification and diagnosis, yet effective disease-modifying therapies remain limited. Disease-specific abnormalities remain essential to clinical interpretation and treatment selection. Existing reviews often focus on individual disorders or isolated mechanisms, leaving the links between shared biology and disease-specific phenotypes insufficiently clear. We synthesize evidence on the epidemiology, risk factors, classification, and pathophysiology of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Huntington's disease, frontotemporal dementia, Friedreich's ataxia, and multiple sclerosis. We compare their clinical manifestations and diagnostic approaches, including the evolving role of biomarkers, and critically assess established and emerging therapies. By distinguishing shared mechanisms from disease-specific abnormalities, we identify key translational gaps and explore how common biological disturbances may lead to distinct clinical trajectories. This cross-disease perspective may inform diagnostic reasoning, treatment development, and future comparative research.
